title: The Five Offspring the Body Brings Forth from its Food
arc: A single act of nourishment, taken into the body, divides into five distinct offspring — breath through the mind, voice through speech, discharge through the lower members, seed through desire, and the somatic child — of which the unregenerate human knows only the last and remains blind to the four interior emissions he is producing in every season.
reading:
This chapter takes a single ordinary fact — that food, when eaten, becomes many things in the body — and reads it as a teaching about the five-fold structure of every reception. What men "gather inward in various likenesses" as food is, correspondentially, every nourishment taken into the natural: truths and goods (or their corrupt counterparts) that the body of man digests. Once inside, that nourishment does not remain one thing. It "habitually disperses forth into five offspring," because the body, like the soul whose form it is, is made to bring forth in the complete five-fold structure of the natural-rational interface.

The first offspring rises through the breath. It comes out of the man on the exhalation, "mounts upon the mind," and proceeds from all his members. This is the offspring at the level of wind and mind — thought itself, the perceptive medium that streams through every part of the natural form whenever a man is alive. It is the most interior of the five emissions: nourishment turned into breath turned into thought, the moving life that pervades the whole organism.

The second offspring comes forth "through the voice and the speech." Here the body's nourishment is brought up one step closer to ultimates: thought given audible form, the mouth as the doorway of expression. What was breath in the first now becomes word.

The third offspring is what "pours forth through the power and the shame" — the body's discharge through its lower members, the waste expelled through the parts that have both capacity and shame attached to them. Read as correspondence, this is the natural's casting-off of what it has used and cannot retain: an outflow at the level of foot and ultimate, the body's involuntary purgation.

The fourth offspring is what is "begotten through the pleasure of desire in males and in females." This is seminal emission, the body's most affection-laden outflow, the product of concupiscence operating in the flesh. It is the offspring on the plane of natural will — the body brings forth in the form of desire's discharge.

The fifth and final offspring is the one "molded and depicted in the flesh," the bodily offspring properly so called — the actual child, the somatic offspring (ⲡⲓⲝⲡⲟ ⲛ̄ⲥⲱⲙⲁⲧⲓⲕⲟⲛ). This is the consummating extension of the series, where the food eaten by the parents is at last shaped and stamped into a new body. It corresponds to the lowest, most ultimate degree of the body's bringing-forth: nourishment fully molded into another natural form.

The pivot of the whole teaching is what comes next. Of these five offspring, the parents know only the last. They recognize the somatic child and pursue it consciously: "they seek after it daily, in every season," from the desire of the heart and from love of progeny. But "the other four offspring they do not perceive; neither are they sick at heart for them, since they are not made manifest to them." This is the spiritual point of the entire chapter. The natural man attends only to the offspring that appears in ultimates — the one he can see, hold, and name as his own. He does not perceive that he is also, in every breath, every word, every discharge, every emission of desire, bringing forth offspring just as truly. Each meal of his life is multiplying into five-fold issue, and four-fifths of that issue passes unnoticed beneath his attention.

Read in the structure of the five faculties, the teaching maps cleanly onto the discrete degrees of the natural-rational form: breath upon mind (the inmost rational), speech (the discursive thought now uttered as teaching), discharge through power (the deliberative or appetitive lower), emission through pleasure (the counsel of the flesh), and the molded child (the reflection-image of the parents stamped in flesh). The body is shown as a complete five-fold generator, every input producing an issue at every degree. But because the unregenerate man lives in his ultimates, he knows only the ultimate offspring; the interior four — what his thought breathes, what his speech bears, what his lower members release, what his desire begets — are hidden from him simply because he has never turned attention to them.

The chapter is therefore a quiet but pointed teaching about spiritual self-knowledge. The body is constantly bringing forth out of what it has received. To regenerate is to begin perceiving the four interior offspring as well as the bodily one — to grow "sick at heart" over the breath, the word, the discharge, and the emission, recognizing that each is a true child of the soul's eating. The visible somatic child is only the ultimate sign of a generative process running at five degrees at once, and the man who sees only the fifth has not yet seen what his own body is doing.

major_images.meaning: Every nourishment received into the natural mind divides into the complete five-fold structure of the natural-rational interface; one reception, five issues at discrete degrees

major_images.image: Breath rising from all members and mounting upon the mind
major_images.meaning: The first and most interior offspring: thought as the wind/perception that pervades the whole organism
The second offspring: thought brought into audible expression at the mouth, the doorway of utterance
The third offspring: the natural's involuntary purgation through its lower members

major_images.image: Seed begotten through pleasure of desire in male and female
major_images.meaning: The fourth offspring: emission on the plane of natural will and concupiscence

major_images.image: The bodily child molded and depicted in the flesh
major_images.meaning: The fifth, somatic offspring — the only one the unregenerate parents consciously perceive and seek

major_images.image: Four offspring not made manifest to their fathers
major_images.meaning: The interior four-fifths of every reception which the natural man, attentive only to ultimates, never perceives himself producing
